CHAPTER 13: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT

INTRODUCTION
- This chapter covers how unemployment is measured in Ireland, its causes, what the government can do to reduce it, and how employment has changed over the last 25 years.
- Study it together with the labour market section of Chapter 9.

FULL EMPLOYMENT AND KEY TERMS
- Full employment is one of the government's economic aims.
- Full employment: everyone who wants a job can find one at existing wage levels.
- An unemployment rate of 4% indicates full employment.
- Zero unemployment is impossible because some people will always be structurally unemployed (need time to retrain, e.g. jobs made obsolete by technology) or frictionally unemployed (between jobs).
- Full employment is usually linked to the PEAK of the business/trade cycle (Chapter 11).
- Workforce: all those who are employed.
- Unemployed: a person who is (i) available for work AND (ii) actively seeking work.
- Labour force: the workforce PLUS the unemployed.
- Unemployment rate: the proportion of the labour force that is unemployed.
  - Formula: Unemployment rate = (number unemployed / labour force) x 100.
- Underemployment (of labour): when a worker's skills or time are not used to their full potential. Examples: a highly qualified family member helping on the family farm; a highly qualified person in an unrelated job that needs no qualifications.

MEASURING UNEMPLOYMENT: LIVE REGISTER AND LABOUR FORCE SURVEY
- Two main methods, which give different figures.
- January 2020: 183,900 people on the Live Register. The Labour Force Survey for Q1 2020 put unemployment at 114,400.

THE LIVE REGISTER
- A count of everyone receiving an unemployment-related social welfare payment, e.g. jobseeker's allowance.
- Why it is not the most accurate measure:
  - Some are in part-time work and legally get a partial payment for days they do not work, but are counted as fully unemployed.
  - A small number work full-time in the hidden economy and illegally claim welfare, yet are counted as unemployed.
  - Some may be 'voluntarily unemployed' - not really actively seeking work.
- It is a count of welfare recipients, not of the truly unemployed, but it does indicate unemployment levels and trends.

THE LABOUR FORCE SURVEY (LFS)
- Introduced in 2017, replacing the Quarterly National Household Survey (QNHS). Seen by many as more accurate.
- The CSO invites 32,500 households each quarter; the achieved sample depends on response. In Q3 2020 there were 12,358 valid responding households - a large sample.
- Participants answer questions about employment status, occupation, etc.
- More accurate because of the large sample, BUT there is a time lag between the quarter surveyed and publication, as results take time to process.

CAUSES / TYPES OF UNEMPLOYMENT
1. Structural unemployment
- A mismatch between the skills of the unemployed and the jobs available.
- Causes: decline of an industry due to changing demand (e.g. peat harvesting in the midlands); jobs made obsolete or replaced by technology (technological unemployment).
- Examples: an unemployed builder cannot apply for a nursing vacancy; a supermarket checkout operator replaced by a self-service checkout.
- Government response: retraining. Example - the 'Just Transition Plan' for Bord na Mona ending peat harvesting in 2020, funding retraining in bog rehabilitation, green energy jobs (e.g. home insulation) and recycling. Bord na Mona no longer harvests peat.
2. Frictional unemployment
- Caused by frictions in the labour market: moving between jobs takes time (ideally someone unemployed on Friday would start a new job on Monday).
- Covers people who are between jobs, whose contract has ended and who are looking for another job, or who have entered the labour force for the first time.
- There is little the government can do, so policies do not generally target it.
3. Seasonal unemployment
- Unemployment at certain times of the year, e.g. tourism workers such as a tour guide or hotel receptionist in winter.
4. Cyclical unemployment
- Unemployment caused by the fall in demand for goods and services in a downturn. Unemployment falls when the economy expands.
- Examples: rose in Ireland in 2008 (financial crisis) and in 2020 (Covid-19).

OTHER FACTORS CONTRIBUTING TO UNEMPLOYMENT
- Rise in the cost of labour: the minimum wage was 10.20 euro an hour in January 2021. An employer with 100 workers at this rate might have employed 200 if it were half. Higher labour costs reduce demand for labour.
- Employers' PRSI: a separate contribution per employee; employers say it discourages hiring by raising labour costs.
- High interest rates: if the ECB raises rates (e.g. to fight inflation), borrowing for investment can fall, slowing the economy and raising unemployment.
- Exchange rates: a rise in the euro against the dollar and sterling makes Irish exports to the US and UK dearer, so demand may fall, and tourism from the US and UK may fall, raising unemployment in hospitality. Class activity: euro moving from 1.20 dollars to 1.40 dollars.
- Uncertainty: after shocks like the 2008 crisis and Covid-19, pessimism cut investment and consumer spending.
- Relocation of multinationals: in 2009 Dell moved 1,900 jobs from Limerick to Poland because of lower costs (e.g. wages) and Polish incentives. The local impact of such closures is huge.

DATA PATTERNS
- The Leaving Cert specification requires investigating labour force data patterns (age, population, gender, location, employment, unemployment). CSO website: statistics, labour market (PxStat lets you make charts).
- Figure 13.1: seasonally adjusted monthly unemployment rate 1998-2020 (both sexes, 15-74). Figure 13.2: people aged 15+ in employment 1998-2019 (thousands).
- These show employment and unemployment are closely aligned to the business cycle.

TRENDS IN IRELAND
1. Mid-1990s to 2007 (Celtic Tiger)
- Unemployment fell and employment rose from the mid-1990s.
- A highly educated labour force and low wages at the end of the 1990s attracted Foreign Direct Investment (FDI). Tax breaks in the International Financial Services Centre (IFSC) in Dublin attracted overseas investment.
- Cutting corporation tax to 12.5% brought more FDI and more direct and indirect jobs. Rising incomes, less emigration and more immigration raised employment further, especially in MNCs and construction, feeding a property boom.
- Construction jobs masked job losses elsewhere. Ireland became expensive and lost competitiveness, so some labour-intensive manufacturing (e.g. textiles) relocated.
- The property boom was fuelled by easy credit and low interest rates after the single currency came in 1999 (euro notes and coins in 2002). The term 'Celtic Tiger' describes the mid-1990s to 2007.
2. 2008 to 2013
- The 2008 crash cut access to credit; banks had huge bad debts; property prices fell; new homes built fell from almost 80,000 in 2006 to 8,500 in 2012, causing construction unemployment.
- Bailing out the banks cost the state 64 billion euro. Unemployment surged to over 15%; emigration rose.
- Consumer spending fell further due to higher taxes and new taxes (USC 2011, LPT 2013); disposable income fell; less credit limited spending and investment.
- The troika (IMF, European Commission and ECB) effectively controlled fiscal policy; the government followed austerity (cutting current spending, raising current revenue).
- A public sector recruitment ban, pay cuts, high taxes and few jobs raised emigration.
- The solution focused on attracting FDI and boosting exports of goods and services.
3. 2013 to 2020
- Recovery: banks slowly lent again; FDI kept rising; exports surged; tourism grew every year, raising hospitality jobs; the property market recovered with more homes, hotels, offices and student accommodation, especially in Dublin.
4. 2020 to 2021
- Covid-19 lockdowns raised unemployment, especially in retail, tourism and hospitality. Activity was severely restricted and consumer spending fell significantly.
- Household savings rose to 125 billion euro by the end of 2020, an increase of over 14 billion that year.

IMPLICATIONS OF UNEMPLOYMENT
1. The economy
- Less consumption: falling disposable incomes cut aggregate demand; workers who fear job losses save more. Demand for both domestic goods and imports (e.g. new cars) falls.
- Less investment: lower demand and pessimism discourage firms from investing or expanding.
2. Government finances
- Higher social welfare costs, e.g. jobseeker's allowance, Housing Assistance Payment (HAP), medical cards.
- Lower revenue from direct and indirect taxes as activity falls.
- The current budget deficit rises (or surplus falls); more borrowing may be needed.
3. Individuals/households
- Emigration rises: unemployment is a push factor. Emigration is also a 'safety valve' - without it, pressure on the welfare system would be huge.
- Brain drain: people educated at the taxpayer's expense leave to work abroad.
4. Household incomes
- Poverty rises as some households cannot afford basics like food and clothing.
- After 2008, many could not pay mortgages after losing jobs; some homes were repossessed.
- Inequality rises as some cannot access healthcare, housing and education.

WHAT THE GOVERNMENT CAN DO TO REDUCE UNEMPLOYMENT
- 1. Cut VAT on certain goods/services, e.g. the 9% rate for tourism and hospitality in 2021.
- 2. Subsidise employers to hire, e.g. JobsPlus gave grants of up to 10,000 euro (2021) to employers hiring people from the Live Register.
- 3. Retraining for the structurally unemployed: the Bord na Mona Just Transition Plan; Springboard, which gives free courses to retrain for sectors with jobs (e.g. IT); schemes encouraging firms to take on apprentices.
- 4. Promote international tourism: Failte Ireland promotes the Wild Atlantic Way, Ireland's Hidden Heartlands and Ireland's Ancient East abroad (developed after the crash).
- 5. Promote exports: a policy that has served Ireland well since the late 1950s.
- 6. Reduce state-imposed business costs, e.g. commercial rates and employers' PRSI.
- 7. Help new businesses with grants and advice, e.g. Enterprise Ireland and County Enterprise Boards.

UNEMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY
- Ireland has signed up to the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs); Global Goal 1 is 'no poverty'.
- CSO evidence shows a strong link between unemployment in a household and poverty. To meet this goal, the government must reduce unemployment.
- The CSO Survey on Income and Living Conditions gives poverty data and the Gini coefficient (0.29 in 2019).

rows.prompt: What is full employment?
options: Every adult in the country is working full-time
The unemployment rate has fallen to exactly zero
All jobs pay at least the minimum wage
Everyone who wants a job can find one at existing wage levels
rows.explanation: Full employment means all who want work can find it at existing wages.

rows.prompt: What unemployment rate indicates full employment, according to the chapter?
rows.explanation: An unemployment rate of 4% indicates full employment.

rows.prompt: Why is zero unemployment unachievable?
options: The minimum wage stops firms hiring every worker
The Live Register always overcounts the unemployed
EU rules set a minimum level of unemployment
Some people will always be between jobs or retraining
rows.explanation: There will always be frictional (between jobs) and structural (retraining) unemployment.

rows.prompt: To be classed as unemployed, a person must be:
options: Receiving jobseeker's allowance and over 25
Available for work and actively seeking work
Registered with the CSO and living in Ireland
Out of work for at least one full year
rows.explanation: Unemployed means (i) available for work and (ii) actively seeking work.

rows.prompt: The labour force is made up of:
options: The workforce only
The unemployed only
The workforce plus the unemployed
All people aged 15 and over
rows.explanation: Labour force = those in the workforce plus those who are unemployed.

rows.prompt: The labour force is 2,000,000 and 100,000 people are unemployed. What is the unemployment rate?
A qualified engineer works in a job that needs no qualifications. This is an example of:
options: Underemployment
Frictional unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
rows.explanation: Underemployment is when a worker's skills or time are not used to their full potential.

rows.prompt: Full employment is usually associated with which phase of the business cycle?
options: The trough
The contraction
The recession
The peak
rows.explanation: The chapter links full employment to the peak of the business/trade cycle.

rows.prompt: What does the Live Register count?
options: Households answering a quarterly CSO survey
People receiving an unemployment-related welfare payment
Workers who have changed jobs during the year
People who have emigrated in the past year
rows.explanation: It counts those receiving payments such as jobseeker's allowance.

rows.prompt: In January 2020, how many people were on the Live Register?
rows.explanation: 183,900 were on the Live Register, while the LFS for Q1 2020 put unemployment at 114,400.

rows.prompt: Why might the Live Register OVERSTATE unemployment?
options: It only counts people who answer the survey each quarter
Part-time workers getting partial payments are counted as unemployed
It leaves out people who claim jobseeker's allowance
It is published with a long time lag
rows.explanation: Part-time workers, some hidden-economy workers and the voluntarily unemployed are all counted.

rows.prompt: The Labour Force Survey replaced which survey in 2017?
options: The Live Register
The Survey on Income and Living Conditions
The Quarterly National Household Survey
The Census of Population
rows.explanation: The LFS replaced the Quarterly National Household Survey (QNHS) in 2017.

rows.prompt: How many households does the CSO invite to take part in the LFS each quarter?
rows.explanation: The CSO invites 32,500 households each quarter.

rows.prompt: What is the main weakness of the Labour Force Survey?
options: There is a time lag before results are published
Its sample size is very small
It counts people working illegally as unemployed
It counts part-time workers as fully unemployed
rows.explanation: Results take time to process, so there is a lag between the quarter and publication.

rows.prompt: A checkout operator is replaced by a self-service checkout. What type of unemployment is this?
options: Seasonal unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Structural (technological) unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
rows.explanation: Jobs replaced by new technology cause structural (technological) unemployment.

rows.prompt: What is the Just Transition Plan an example of?
options: A subsidy to reduce seasonal unemployment
A tax cut to reduce cyclical unemployment
A tourism campaign to reduce frictional unemployment
Retraining to reduce structural unemployment
rows.explanation: It funded retraining of Bord na Mona workers after peat harvesting ended.

rows.prompt: A school leaver looking for a first job is an example of:
options: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
rows.explanation: Frictional unemployment includes those entering the labour force for the first time.

rows.prompt: Why do government policies generally not target frictional unemployment?
options: It is the largest type of unemployment
There is little the government can do about it
It only affects workers in tourism
It is caused by EU rules
rows.explanation: The chapter states there is little the government can do to address it.

rows.prompt: A hotel receptionist loses their job every winter. This is:
options: Seasonal unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Structural unemployment
Technological unemployment
rows.explanation: Seasonal unemployment happens at certain times of year, e.g. tourism in winter.

rows.prompt: Unemployment caused by falling demand in an economic downturn is called:
options: Cyclical unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
Structural unemployment
rows.explanation: Cyclical unemployment rose in 2008 and 2020 due to downturns.

rows.prompt: How could a rise in the minimum wage increase unemployment?
options: It lowers the cost of labour, so firms hire fewer people
It raises the cost of labour, reducing demand for workers
It increases the money supply, so prices fall
It raises exports, so firms need fewer workers
rows.explanation: An increase in the cost of labour reduces the demand for labour.

rows.prompt: The euro rises from $1.20 to $1.40. What is the likely effect on Irish employment?
options: It rises, as Irish exports become cheaper in the US
It rises, as more US tourists visit Ireland
It falls, as exports dearer and US tourism declines
It is unaffected, as Ireland uses the euro
rows.explanation: A stronger euro raises the price of exports and can reduce tourism, raising unemployment.

rows.prompt: In 2009 Dell moved 1,900 jobs from Limerick to which country?
options: Germany
Poland
France
Spain
rows.explanation: Dell relocated to Poland due to lower production costs and Polish incentives.

rows.prompt: How could higher ECB interest rates increase unemployment?
options: Saving falls, so banks have more to lend
The euro weakens, so exports collapse
Borrowing for investment falls, slowing the economy
Government spending automatically rises
rows.explanation: Higher rates reduce borrowing for investment, slowing the economy and raising unemployment.

rows.prompt: Which helped attract FDI to Ireland in the late 1990s?
options: High corporation tax and high wages
A falling population and rising emigration
A highly educated labour force and low wages
Strict limits on bank lending
rows.explanation: A highly educated workforce, low wages, IFSC tax breaks and 12.5% corporation tax attracted FDI.

rows.prompt: New home completions fell from almost 80,000 in 2006 to about how many in 2012?
rows.explanation: Construction of new homes fell to 8,500 units in 2012.

rows.prompt: What did bailing out the banks cost the state?
options: €13 billion
€125 billion
€64 billion
€14 billion
rows.explanation: The cost to the state of bailing out the banks was €64 billion.

rows.prompt: During the 2020 lockdowns, household savings rose to €125bn. What does this show?
options: Consumer spending fell sharply while activity was restricted
Banks stopped accepting deposits from households
Consumer spending rose to a record high
DIRT was abolished during the pandemic
rows.explanation: With restricted activity, consumer spending fell and savings rose by over €14bn in 2020.

rows.prompt: Why is emigration described as a 'safety valve'?
options: It reduces pressure on the social welfare system
It increases the number of skilled workers at home
It raises government tax revenue in a recession
It stops the brain drain of graduates
rows.explanation: If all the unemployed stayed, the pressure on welfare would be huge.

rows.prompt: The JobsPlus scheme helps reduce unemployment by:
options: Giving free IT courses to people who want to retrain
Promoting the Wild Atlantic Way to tourists abroad
Cutting VAT for the hospitality sector to 9%
Giving grants to employers who hire people from the Live Register
rows.explanation: JobsPlus gave grants of up to €10,000 to employers hiring people from the Live Register.

rows.prompt: Which SDG links to the effects of unemployment discussed in the chapter?
options: Global Goal 1: no poverty
Global Goal 13: climate action
Global Goal 4: quality education
Global Goal 6: clean water
rows.explanation: CSO evidence shows a strong link between household unemployment and poverty.

rows.prompt: Distinguish between the workforce and the labour force, and give the formula for the unemployment rate.
rows.model_answer: The workforce is all those who are employed. The labour force is the workforce plus the unemployed (those available for and actively seeking work). Unemployment rate = number unemployed / labour force x 100.

rows.prompt: Name the two methods used to measure unemployment in Ireland and say which is more accurate.
rows.model_answer: The Live Register and the Labour Force Survey (LFS). The LFS is more accurate because it surveys a large sample of households (12,358 valid responses in Q3 2020) about their actual employment status. The Live Register only counts those receiving unemployment-related payments, including some part-time and hidden-economy workers.

rows.prompt: Explain structural and frictional unemployment, with an example of each.
rows.model_answer: Structural unemployment is a mismatch between the skills of the unemployed and the jobs available, e.g. peat workers after Bord na Mona stopped harvesting, or a checkout operator replaced by a self-service till. Frictional unemployment is people between jobs or entering the labour force for the first time, e.g. someone whose contract has ended.

rows.prompt: Explain seasonal and cyclical unemployment.
rows.model_answer: Seasonal unemployment happens at certain times of the year, e.g. a tour guide out of work in winter. Cyclical unemployment comes from falling demand in an economic downturn, e.g. the rise in unemployment in 2008 and in 2020 with Covid-19.

rows.prompt: State three factors, other than the four types, that can contribute to unemployment.
rows.model_answer: A rise in the cost of labour, such as a higher minimum wage or employers' PRSI, reduces demand for workers. Higher ECB interest rates cut borrowing for investment and slow the economy. A stronger euro makes exports dearer and reduces tourism; uncertainty and MNC relocation (e.g. Dell moving 1,900 jobs to Poland) also matter.

rows.prompt: Describe what happened to employment in Ireland between 2008 and 2013 and why.
rows.model_answer: The 2008 crash cut credit, property prices fell and house building fell from almost 80,000 to 8,500 units, causing construction job losses. Unemployment rose above 15% and emigration increased. Austerity under the troika, new taxes like the USC and a public sector recruitment ban further cut spending and jobs.

rows.prompt: Outline three implications of high unemployment.
rows.model_answer: Consumption and investment fall as disposable incomes drop and pessimism grows. Government finances worsen as welfare costs rise and tax revenue falls, increasing the deficit. Emigration and brain drain increase, and poverty and inequality rise as households struggle to afford basics, with some homes repossessed.

rows.prompt: State four actions the government could take to reduce unemployment.
rows.model_answer: Cut VAT on some services, e.g. the 9% rate for hospitality. Give employers hiring subsidies like JobsPlus. Fund retraining such as Springboard courses or the Just Transition Plan. Promote tourism (e.g. the Wild Atlantic Way) and exports, reduce business costs like employers' PRSI, and support new businesses through Enterprise Ireland.

rows.prompt: (a) Explain the term 'unemployed'. (b) Distinguish between the Live Register and the Labour Force Survey as measures of unemployment, and state which is more accurate. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: (a) A person is unemployed if they are available for work and actively seeking work. (b) The Live Register counts everyone receiving an unemployment-related social welfare payment, such as jobseeker's allowance. It is less accurate because part-time workers getting partial payments are counted as fully unemployed, some people working in the hidden economy illegally claim payments, and some may be voluntarily unemployed. In January 2020 it showed 183,900 people. The Labour Force Survey, introduced in 2017 to replace the QNHS, surveys households (32,500 invited each quarter; 12,358 valid responses in Q3 2020) about their actual employment status. It gave 114,400 unemployed in Q1 2020. The LFS is more accurate because of its large sample, although there is a time lag before results are published.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) 4m (2m + 2m). (b) Live Register explained 5m; LFS explained 5m; more accurate method named and justified 6m (2m statement + 4m reasons).

rows.prompt: Explain the four types of unemployment and outline one government measure to reduce each type where possible. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: Structural unemployment is a mismatch between skills and available jobs, from industry decline (peat harvesting) or technology (self-service checkouts). The government can fund retraining, e.g. the Just Transition Plan and Springboard courses. Frictional unemployment covers people between jobs or entering the labour force for the first time; there is little the government can do about it. Seasonal unemployment occurs at certain times of year, e.g. tourism workers in winter; the government can support the sector by promoting international tourism, such as the Wild Atlantic Way, and by cutting VAT for tourism and hospitality. Cyclical unemployment comes from falling demand in a downturn, as in 2008 and 2020; the government can boost demand by cutting VAT (e.g. 9% for hospitality) or giving hiring subsidies like JobsPlus.
rows.marking_scheme: 4 types x 4m (2m explanation + 2m example) = 16m. Government measures: 3 x 3m = 9m (frictional - recognising little can be done earns marks).

rows.prompt: Discuss the economic implications of high unemployment for (i) the government's finances and (ii) individuals and households. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) Social welfare costs rise as more people qualify for jobseeker's allowance, the Housing Assistance Payment and medical cards. Revenue from direct taxes falls as fewer people earn, and indirect tax revenue falls as spending drops. The current budget deficit rises, or a surplus falls, and the government may need to borrow more. (ii) Emigration rises as unemployment is a push factor; it acts as a safety valve but causes a brain drain of people educated at taxpayers' expense. Poverty rises as households struggle to buy food and clothing. After 2008, many could not pay their mortgages and some homes were repossessed. Inequality rises as some households struggle to access healthcare, housing and education.
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 2 points x 5m (2m statement + 3m explanation). (ii) 2 points x 5m (2m + 3m).

rows.prompt: Outline the factors that caused changes in employment in Ireland during (i) the Celtic Tiger period and (ii) the recovery from 2013 to 2020. (15 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) A highly educated labour force and low wages in the late 1990s attracted FDI, helped by IFSC tax breaks and the cut in corporation tax to 12.5%. Rising incomes, less emigration and more immigration raised employment, especially in MNCs and construction. Easy credit and low interest rates after the euro came in fuelled a property boom. (ii) Banks slowly began to lend again, FDI kept rising and exports surged. Tourism grew every year, creating hospitality jobs, and construction of homes, hotels, offices and student accommodation recovered, especially in Dublin.
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 3 points x 3m (1m statement + 2m explanation) = 9m. (ii) 2 points x 3m = 6m.
